query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the lamellar microstructure of eutectic high-entropy alloys by tailored cryo-rolling and annealing will simultaneously increase strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a typical, coarser lamellar dual-phase (ductile FCC + reinforcing B2) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a processing route based on cryo-rolling followed by annealing to refine the lamellar spacing and promote an interpenetrating network between the ductile and reinforcing phases.
generation.conditions: Testing under room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading conditions typical of structural applications; processing parameters similar to those used in literature for cryogenic deformation and subsequent annealing.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchically refined lamellar architecture characterized by reduced lamellar spacing and improved phase connectivity between the ductile FCC phase and the hard B2 phase.
generation.mechanism: Refined lamellar spacing enhances strain partitioning between the two phases, delays crack initiation, and facilitates dislocation motion. This balanced microstructural configuration enhances the work-hardening ability of the alloy, leading to simultaneous improvements in strength (due to finer structural features and more effective load transfer) and ductility (via improved strain accommodation).
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in yield strength (for example, from approximately 1.2 GPa to around 1.47 GPa) along with an improvement in ductility (from about 12% elongation to near 14%), relative to conventionally processed alloys.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloys processed by traditional cold-rolling and annealing that exhibit lower strength (~1.2 GPa) and ductility (~12%).
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be significant in eutectic HEAs with dual-phase (FCC+B2) microstructures similar to AlCoCrFeNi2.1; the results may differ for HEAs with different phase distributions or compositions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement and the universality of the mechanism across various eutectic HEA compositions remain to be fully validated; additional factors such as dislocation interactions may also contribute.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples: one processed by conventional cold-rolling and annealing, and one processed by cryo-rolling followed by annealing intended to refine the lamellar architecture. Characterize the microstructures using electron microscopy to quantify lamellar spacing and phase connectivity, and perform quasi-static tensile testing at room temperature to measure yield strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled and annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and ductility over the conventional processing route, or if the expected refined lamellar microstructure is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. The present study for the first time demonstrated that cryo-deformation and annealing could be a novel microstructural design strategy for overcoming strength-ductility trade off in multiphase high ent

In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.

frame.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloys in their typical dual-phase (eutectic) state, consisting of a ductile matrix with a second, often brittle, reinforcing phase.
frame.goal: Achieve a simultaneous improvement in both strength and ductility for structural applications.
frame.limitation: The conventional trade-off where enhancement of strength (typically via microstructural refinement or hardening) generally leads to reduced ductility.
constraints: Single intervention (i.e., one change in processing, composition, or microstructure)
Must be applicable to eutectic HEAs designed for structural use
frame.regime: Room temperature or service-condition mechanical testing conditions typical of load-bearing structural components.
prior_attempts: Traditional approaches like alloying adjustments or heat treatments have been used, but they often improve one property while detrimentally affecting the other.

Microstructural refinements in other alloy systems have attempted to break the strength-ductility trade-off, but these methods either complicate processing or fail to reach simultaneous enhancement in HEAs.

families.principle: Intentionally designing the microstructural arrangement—such as the phase distribution, lamellar spacing, and interface connectivity—can optimize load partitioning and delay material failure, fostering a balance between strength and ductility.
cues_for: eutectic high-entropy alloys in their typical dual-phase state
families.best_lever: Engineer the eutectic architecture to achieve an optimal lamellar spacing and interpenetrating network between the ductile matrix and the reinforcing phase, maximizing strain partitioning and delaying crack initiation under load.

families.principle: Modifying the processing parameters (e.g., cooling rate, solidification conditions) changes the kinetics of phase formation and the resultant microstructure, potentially optimizing phase spacing and morphology.
cues_against: Prior attempts with heat treatments have been employed, suggesting that simplistic processing tweaks might have been tried already
families.best_lever: Alter the cooling rate during solidification (for example, through rapid solidification techniques) to control the eutectic lamellar spacing and thereby synergistically tailor the phase morphology.

families.principle: Altering the atomic species and their proportions can modify phase stability, solid‐solution strengthening, and the nature of interfaces between the ductile and reinforcing phases.
cues_against: Traditional approaches like alloying adjustments have been used and often improve one property at the expense of the other
families.best_lever: Introduce a minor alloying element that preferentially stabilizes a tougher, well-bonded interface between the two phases without compromising the inherent strength of the reinforcing phase.

families.principle: Modifying the chemistry or structure at the phase boundaries can improve interfacial bonding, reduce crack nucleation, and enable better dislocation transfer, which may balance both strength and ductility.
cues_for: simultaneous improvement in strength and ductility
cues_against: The bulk dual-phase eutectic structure is the primary design cue, and surface/interface modifications might be challenging to implement uniformly throughout the volume
families.best_lever: Enhance the interfacial cohesion between the ductile and brittle phases, perhaps by local compositional tuning at the interfaces or introducing an interfacial agent during solidification to strengthen the boundary.

families.principle: Carefully designed heat treatments or deformation schedules can influence precipitate formation and relieve residual stresses, impacting both strength and ductility.
cues_for: mechanism of simultaneously improving strength and ductility
cues_against: Traditional heat treatments have been applied in prior attempts but typically lead to an improvement in one property at the expense of the other
families.best_lever: Implement an unconventional thermomechanical processing route that might induce beneficial precipitate distributions while refining the microstructure, though previous methods make this a less promising route.
